course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Globalization
unit.description: Study how technology, disease, and environmental change reshaped the world, how the global economy and culture developed, and how people and institutions responded to globalization.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

choices: agriculture and food processing

questions.prompt: Reagan's economic policies differed from the New Deal in that Reagan
choices: expanded government regulation of business
sought to reduce government's economic role

nationalized major industries such as steel

He cut taxes and regulation; the New Deal expanded government.

questions.prompt: Reagan's purpose in this passage was most likely to
choices: justify reducing government spending and taxes
propose new government jobs programs
praise the strong economy of the 1970s
call for higher taxes on all Americans
questions.explanation: He blames taxes, spending, and government for economic problems.
choiceExplanations: He blames taxes, spending, and government for economic problems.
He says government is not the solution.
He calls the economy afflicted.
He calls the tax burden too heavy.
questions.distinguisher: Reagan proposes removing roadblocks, not creating programs.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Ronald Reagan, president of the United States, inaugural address, January 20, 1981
stimulusBlocks.citation: Ronald Reagan, Inaugural Address, January 20, 1981. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (inaugural/1981-Reagan.txt).
stimulusBlocks.note: The transcript used to check this excerpt ends the third paragraph's sentence at “problem”; as delivered, Reagan continued, “government is the problem.” In 1980, US inflation was above 12 percent.
stimulusBlocks.text:
These United States are confronted with an economic affliction of great proportions. We suffer from the longest and one of the worst sustained inflations in our national history. . . .

But great as our tax burden is, it has not kept pace with public spending. For decades, we have piled deficit upon deficit, mortgaging our future and our children's future for the temporary convenience of the present. . . .

In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem . . . .

In the days ahead I will propose removing the roadblocks that have slowed our economy and reduced productivity.

questions.prompt: Reagan's speech is best understood in the context of
choices: the Great Depression and mass unemployment of the 1930s
high inflation and slow growth in the 1970s
the Marshall Plan's aid to Western Europe
the end of the Cold War and the Soviet collapse
questions.explanation: Inflation above 12 percent shaped his argument.
choiceExplanations: The Depression ended four decades earlier.
Inflation above 12 percent shaped his argument.
The Marshall Plan was in 1948.
The Cold War ended after 1989.
questions.distinguisher: The Depression was a crisis of falling prices; Reagan faced rising prices.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, Deng Xiaoping's reforms
choices: ended Communist Party rule in the countryside
let peasants sell surplus crops at market prices
privatized state companies such as British Telecom
banned foreign investment in special zones
questions.explanation: Market prices gave peasants incentives to produce more.
choiceExplanations: The party kept its monopoly.
Market prices gave peasants incentives to produce more.
That was Thatcher.
Special zones invited investment.
questions.distinguisher: Deng's reforms were economic; the party kept political control.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 9.4 key concept: some states adopted free-market economic policies in the late twentieth century
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing free-market reforms, 1973–1991
stimulusBlocks.text:
After 1979, British prime minister Margaret Thatcher sold state-owned companies such as British Telecom to private investors and limited the power of labor unions. In Chile, economists trained in the United States advised the military government of Augusto Pinochet to cut tariffs and privatize industries.

In China, Deng Xiaoping allowed peasants to sell surplus crops at market prices and opened special economic zones to foreign investment after 1978. China's economy grew by roughly 10 percent a year for three decades, while the Communist Party kept its monopoly on political power.

questions.prompt: The reforms in Britain, Chile, and China described in the passage were similar in that all
choices: were carried out by democratic governments
expanded the role of markets
nationalized major industries
were led by communist parties
questions.explanation: Each moved toward markets and private enterprise.
choiceExplanations: Chile had a military government and China a one-party state.
Each moved toward markets and private enterprise.
They privatized industries.
Only China was communist.
questions.distinguisher: Only Britain was a democracy; Chile and China were not.

questions.prompt: The passage would best support which argument about economic reform?
choices: Market reforms happened only in democracies
Market reforms spread under different political systems
Market reforms ended China's economic growth
Market reforms began in China and spread to Britain
questions.explanation: Democratic Britain, military Chile, and communist China all adopted them.
choiceExplanations: Chile and China were not democracies.
Democratic Britain, military Chile, and communist China all adopted them.
China grew about 10 percent a year.
Thatcher's reforms began in 1979, Deng's in 1978, independently.
questions.distinguisher: China and Britain reformed around the same time, but neither copied the other.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the Asian Tigers grew by
choices: producing goods for export
closing their economies to trade
relying only on farming
avoiding investment in education
choiceExplanations: Export-led industry drove their growth.
They depended on trade.
They industrialized.
They invested heavily in education.
questions.distinguisher: The passage says they invested heavily in education.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 9.4 key concept: new economic centers developed in Asia, and multinational corporations shifted production around the world
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the rise of new Asian economies, 1960–2000
stimulusBlocks.text:
From the 1960s, South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Singapore grew rapidly by producing goods for export. These Asian Tigers began with textiles and toys and moved into steel, ships, and electronics, investing heavily in education.

Multinational corporations moved factories to countries where wages were lower and shifted research and design to cities with skilled workers. Wealthy countries increasingly built knowledge economies, in which more people worked in finance, technology, and services than in manufacturing.

questions.prompt: The shift described in the passage most likely contributed to
choices: fewer factory jobs in older industrial regions
the breakup of large multinational corporations
a long decline in the volume of world trade
the end of the Asian Tigers' growth in the 1960s
choiceExplanations: Production moved to lower-wage countries.
Corporations grew.
World trade grew as production spread.
Their growth began in the 1960s and continued.
questions.distinguisher: The 1960s marked the start, not the end, of the Tigers' growth.
